//: The curated register of everything Chrono Mock ships that somebody else wrote. This file is the SOURCE, not a report: the SBOM attached to a release is generated FROM it, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md carries the same set with the full licence texts, and `chrono license --components` prints it for a user with no internet. One register, three renderings.
//why-not-a-scan: A scanner run over the built package would be the obvious alternative and is the wrong tool. It reads what packaging left behind rather than what went in, it cannot tell a build-time crate from a linked one, and it assigns licences by guessing from file names. The job of a scan here is to POLICE this register, not to replace it: `crates/cli/tests/components.rs` checks every rust-crate entry against Cargo.lock in both directions, and `packaging/build-dist.ps1` checks every managed entry against the deps.json the publish actually produced.
//how-versions-are-kept-true: Every version below is declared here and checked against the build. A dependency bump therefore fails a gate until this file is updated, which is the point - an SBOM that quietly describes a different build than the one in the zip is worse than none. Measured on 2026-09-08: THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md had gone stale at `log 0.4.33` while the shipped binary carried 0.4.34, and nothing noticed for a week.
//packages: The two things a release publishes. A component belongs to one or both, and each gets its own SBOM - a single document describing both would misstate each.

cli.description: The command line tool: both native cores, both injected libraries, the calendars and the presets

gui.description: The window, self-contained, with the same native cores underneath it

//components: kind is how the thing arrives: rust-crate is compiled into our binaries from crates.io, vendored-c is third-party C source compiled into one of them, nuget is a prebuilt managed assembly, dotnet-runtime-pack is part of the self-contained .NET runtime the GUI carries. license_declared is what the component itself states, license_concluded is the option we take under it - the difference is the whole reason SPDX has two fields.

components.name: MinHook
components.//: Not a package of its own on any registry: the `minhook` crate above vendors this C library and compiles it into chrono_hook.dll. It is listed separately because its licence differs from the crate that carries it, which is exactly what a scan of the built DLL would miss.
components.//version: The vendored source disagrees with itself, and this records which number we took and why. Its CMakeLists.txt still sets 1.3.3 while its own README version history has v1.3.4 (28 Mar 2025) at the top, so the snapshot carries 1.3.4 and the build file was not bumped upstream. Checked in the crate source on 2026-09-08, at minhook-0.9.0/minhook/.

components.name: Hacker Disassembler Engine
components.//: Bundled inside MinHook (its src/hde/), so it arrives two levels down from anything we declared: a crate that vendors a C library that vendors a disassembler. Its own copyright holder and its own notice, which is why it is a component here rather than a footnote. It ships no version of its own, and NOASSERTION is what SPDX has for that - better than inventing one.

components.name: WPF-UI
components.supplier: Leszek Pomianowski and WPF UI Contributors
components.//: Ships as Wpf.Ui.dll. Its embedded fonts are FluentSystemIcons (MIT) - re-check that on every version bump, the note in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md says how.

components.name: WPF-UI.Abstractions
components.supplier: Leszek Pomianowski and WPF UI Contributors

components.name: Microsoft.NETCore.App.Runtime.win-x64
components.//: The base runtime the self-contained window carries. Its version is decided by the SDK on the machine that publishes, and global.json does not pin the SDK - so the packaging script checks this line against the deps.json the publish produced and stops if they differ.

components.name: Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime.win-x64
components.//: WPF itself, which is what makes the window a window.

components.name: Microsoft.Windows.SDK.NET.Ref
components.//: Ships as Microsoft.Windows.SDK.NET.dll and WinRT.Runtime.dll - the Windows projections the desktop runtime pack pulls in.
components.//licence: 🔴 The one component here that is NOT under an SPDX licence, and the reason this register is read from the package rather than assumed. Its nuspec carries no <license type="expression"> at all - only a licenseUrl pointing at the Windows SDK licence terms. SPDX has LicenseRef- for exactly this: a licence with no identifier. Checked in the nuspec on 2026-09-08, after an earlier draft of this file had written MIT from memory and been wrong.
